Lessons.Title: Using Trigonometric Ratios to Find Angles
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: recover acute right-triangle angle measures from valid side ratios using inverse sine, inverse cosine and inverse tangent, distinguishing inverse functions from reciprocals.
Teacher source introduces inverse-function notation and ladder geometry with degree-level rounding. Maintain input restriction 0<opposite/hypotenuse<1 for a genuine nondegenerate acute angle.

Teacher rubric (0–8): four human 0/1/2 criteria cover right-triangle inverse-function correspondence and degree mode, exact source 3-4-5 angles and END triangle, original 4:1 ladder versus 13ft/12ft geometry with safety context, and nine source Practice items with honest figure limitations.

Original Edulytiks instruction and examples aligned to Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 4, CC BY 4.0. No publisher logos, artwork or restricted assessment content included.

Source 9.1 Once More with the Table (10 min): original right triangle side lengths3,4,5. Use ratio opposite/adjacent3/4 to find acute angle theta=arctan(3/4)≈36.87° rounded37°; complementary acute53.13° rounded53°. Compare right-triangle table estimate and other arcsin/arccos calculations. IMPORTANT: arctan, arcsin, arccos yield an angle from ratio; 'tan^-1' on calculator is inverse FUNCTION, not numerical reciprocal 1/tan. Use DEGREE mode and reasonable integer-degree reporting.

Source 9.2 From Ratios to Angles (10 min): independently labelled three source right triangles ask students to find missing sides and angles, use inverse trig only with appropriate real side ratio and correct right angle; drawings in accessible source text lack all numerical labels, so teacher verifies source figure before assigning original values. Compare Pythagoras, complementary-angle sum and multiple inverse-trig equations with partners, explaining why angles are unique for a valid acute ratio.

Source 9.3 Leaning Ladders (15 min): source historical classroom approximation body height:arm reach =4:1 (vertical:horizontal) implies ground angle arctan4≈75.96° (about76°). For a 13-ft straight ladder to reach a roof 12ft high exactly at roof top, ground offset sqrt(13²-12²)=5ft and ground angle arcsin(12/13)≈67.38°, different from 76°. To place 12ft of vertical rise at source 4:1 guideline needs horizontal3ft and along-ladder length sqrt(12²+3²)=sqrt153≈12.37ft, so 13-ft ladder can extend past contact point in this simplified model. Source asks students to reason if feasible and give instructions, not to certify actual safe use. A 5:1 ratio corresponds about78.69°, different from the source 4:1 rough heuristic. Any ladder deployment must comply with current product/safety rules, secure footing and trained supervision; classroom ratio is NOT a standalone safety authorization.

Source lesson synthesis: inverse sine, inverse cosine, inverse tangent correspond opposite/hyp, adjacent/hyp and opposite/adj for a specified acute right triangle; arccos/arcsin inputs are strictly between0 and1 for nondegenerate acute angle, arctan positive. Source triangle END d18, n22: e=sqrt(22²-18²)=sqrt160≈12.649; theta=arccos(18/22)≈35.10° and alpha complementary≈54.90°, source rounds e≈12.6, theta35°, alpha55°. Student summary opposite3 adjacent12 -> angle arctan(3/12)≈14.04° and other75.96°.

Source Practice P1-P9: P1 parking garage maximum incline8.5° is a SOURCE CLASSROOM criterion, actual incline figure missing so no verified safe/unsafe choice. P2 ABCD rectangle diagonal AC and angles alpha/theta source image dependent; P3 missing measures source diagram dependent. P4 trigonometric choice equations sin27=x/15, cos63=y/15, tan27=y/x, sin63=x/15, tan63=y/x require original figure orientation; cannot infer truth values just from expressions. P5 sin30=cos(theta) -> theta60° choice C. P6 3.5m tent rope making17° with ground means height3.5sin17 choice C. P7 source unknown x figure dependent. P8 find missing sides original source figure dependent, verify by second method. P9 original triangle XYZ onto BCA rigid-motion sequence needs original labelled drawings. Original protected 9.4 Cool-down Again with the Calculator not accessible, use independent first-party two-sides-angle proof and explanation.

Source constraints: 4:1 'safe' ladder and 8.5-degree 'safe' parking garage are curricular modelling claims, not established modern legal safety standards. Record units, actual measurement uncertainty, and any physical restrictions. Do not merge with shared engines or claim Stage D teacher grade saved.

KeyConcepts.Title: Inverse sine
KeyConcepts.Definition: For 0<r<1, arcsin(r) is the unique acute angle with sine r.
KeyConcepts.Rule: θ=arcsin(opposite/hypotenuse) when the ratio is between 0 and 1.

KeyConcepts.Title: Inverse cosine
KeyConcepts.Definition: For 0<r<1, arccos(r) returns the acute angle with cosine r.

KeyConcepts.Title: Inverse tangent
KeyConcepts.Definition: For any positive leg ratio r>0, arctan(r) gives the unique acute angle with tangent r.

WorkedExamples.Title: Recover angle from leg lengths
WorkedExamples.Question: A right triangle has opposite=3 and adjacent=4 for angle θ. Find θ.
Steps: Check both legs positive and right triangle defined.

WorkedExamples.Title: Use inverse sine safely
WorkedExamples.Question: Opposite side is 5 and hypotenuse 13 in a right triangle. Find acute angle.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use arcsin in its acute domain.
Steps: Because 0<5/13<1, the acute inverse sine exists.
Check 13 is the longest side and adjacent leg=12 by Pythagoras.
WorkedExamples.Check: If opposite/hypotenuse exceeded 1, the right-triangle measurements would be invalid.

WorkedExamples.Title: A ladder's angle
WorkedExamples.Question: A straight ladder 10 m long reaches 8 m vertically against a wall on level ground. What is its angle with ground?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use sine of angle at ground.
Steps: Ladder is the hypotenuse 10 m, wall height is opposite leg 8 m.
Ground offset is √(10²−8²)=6 m and tanθ=8/6≈1.333.
WorkedExamples.Check: No safety recommendation follows from this simplified wall model.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Inverse function returns an angle; reciprocal cosecant returns a number.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use arcsin for angle recovery and check degree mode.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Taking arccos of ratio greater than 1
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Cosine of an acute angle in a right triangle is between 0 and 1.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Reject impossible input measurements instead of inventing a real angle.

SummaryPoints: Learning goal: recover acute right-triangle angle measures from valid side ratios using inverse sine, inverse cosine and inverse tangent, distinguishing inverse functions from reciprocals.
Choose correct trigonometric ratios and valid domains; label precise units and approximations.
A complete representation or modelling proof needs teacher review, not a machine-scored scalar.

Lessons.Title: Solving Problems with Trigonometry
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: decompose polygons into right triangles and solve real-world path/height problems with dimensionally consistent trigonometric equations and units.
The official student sequence connects inscribed regular polygons and a realistic descent context; first-party examples preserve the mathematical operations but not publisher photographs.

Teacher rubric (0–8): four teacher-scored 0/1/2 criteria require independent regular inscribed polygon constructions with exact and approximate n-gon perimeters, consistent miles-to-feet aircraft descent equation and path, source area/similarity polygon transfer, and eight source Practice including cautious safety/image limits.

Original Edulytiks instruction and examples aligned to Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 4, CC BY 4.0. No publisher logos, artwork or restricted assessment content included.

Source 10.1 Notice and Wonder Practicing Perimeter (5 min): show several independently drawn regular polygons inscribed in a circle radius1, ask students to observe how many sides and what happens to perimeter BEFORE any formula. Record correct definition every polygon vertex on circumference, and distinguish circle inscribed inside polygon (tangent to its sides). Do not claim a publisher interactive polygon applet is connected or that a finite polygon equals the circumference.

Source 10.2 Growing Regular Polygons (20 min): original circle radius1 metre, determine PERIMETERS of inscribed square, regular pentagon and decagon by drawing the centre, two adjacent radii and an altitude to split the central isosceles triangle into two right triangles. For regular n-gon, central half-angle=180/n degrees, half side=sin(180/n)*1 metre, perimeter P_n=2n*sin(180/n) metres. Source square P4=4sqrt2≈5.657m, pentagon P5=10sin36≈5.878m, decagon P10=20sin18≈6.180m. Compare against 2pi≈6.283m and note inscribed polygon perimeter approaches circumference from below as n increases; record student peer-revised explanation, not just numerical values.

Source 10.2 optional extension: unit-radius outer circle has square inscribed inside of side sqrt2, so its own inscribed smaller circle radius sqrt2/2 and perimeter pi*sqrt2. Difference of outer and inner circumference=2pi-pi*sqrt2=pi(2-sqrt2) metres. Increasing number of regular polygon sides makes difference between corresponding inscribed/circumscribed circle radii smaller, approaching0; source asks for qualitative explanation.

Source 10.3 Gentle Descent (10 min): original airplane horizontal leg150 MILES and vertical drop35,000 FEET. Convert 150 miles=792,000 feet or drop35000/5280≈6.62879 miles BEFORE ratio; descent angle=arctan(35000/792000)≈2.53 degrees, straight flight path=sqrt(150²+(35000/5280)²)≈150.146 miles. Distinguish flight path from horizontal ground displacement. State straight planar ray idealization and assumptions; real aircraft trajectories can differ.

Source lesson synthesis 10.4: source first-party regular hexagon with SIDE10 units decomposed into six equilateral side10 triangles of altitude5sqrt3 and area25sqrt3 each, total150sqrt3≈259.808 square units (source rounds259.8); retain previous independent Edulytiks worked example hexagon side4 area24sqrt3. Original Again with Area Cool-down teacher-login locked; independently authored teacher-scored symbolic polygon calculation and air-unit conversion are appropriate instead.

Source Practice P1-P8: P1 area of original pictured isosceles trapezoid requires actual diagram with dimensions/angles, no fabricated number. P2 tree shadow12ft, sun altitude62 degrees gives height12tan62 feet≈22.57. P3 plane ascent6 degrees over horizontal10 miles gives rise10tan6 miles≈1.051 and straight path10/cos6≈10.055 miles. P4 source inverse-trig triangle marked values unavailable. P5 source parking garage 8.5-degree max classroom angle needs source ramp figure; do not claim real safety compliance. P6 true complementary identities A cos37=sin53, C sin37=cos53, E cos(theta)=sin(90-theta), choices A C E, B and D false. P7 30ft kite string at27 degrees gives height30sin27≈13.62ft, choice B13.6ft. P8 original square diagonal length picture requires labels. Source keeps figures, reasoning, reasonable precision and unit sensitivity human-scored.

KeyConcepts.Title: Composite regular polygons
KeyConcepts.Definition: Regular hexagon of side s is six equilateral triangles of side s.

KeyConcepts.Title: Descent angle
KeyConcepts.Definition: A straight path drops vertical height h while traversing horizontal distance d>0.
KeyConcepts.Rule: tanθ=h/d where θ is depression from horizontal.

KeyConcepts.Title: Dimensional conversion
KeyConcepts.Definition: Convert feet and miles to one system before computing a trigonometric ratio.
KeyConcepts.Example: If horizontal run=150 miles and drop=35,000 ft, ratio=35,000/(150×5280).

WorkedExamples.Title: Polygon decomposition
WorkedExamples.Question: Find the area of a regular hexagon with side length 4 cm.
WorkedExamples.Method: Split it into six equilateral triangles.
Steps: The six central angles are 360°/6=60°, so six central triangles are equilateral.
Approximate A≈41.57 cm² if a decimal is needed.
WorkedExamples.Check: Do not multiply linear side lengths without square units.

WorkedExamples.Title: Descent angle with unit conversion
WorkedExamples.Question: An airplane descends 35,000 ft while travelling 150 miles horizontally. Find descent angle from horizontal.
WorkedExamples.Method: Convert distance and use inverse tangent.
Steps: Distinguish horizontal travel distance from actual straight-line flight path.
WorkedExamples.Check: 35,000 feet divided by 150 miles without conversion is dimensionally invalid.

WorkedExamples.Title: Flight-path hypotenuse
WorkedExamples.Question: For the same idealized descent, compute the straight path length in miles.
WorkedExamples.Check: Assumes straight-line motion and planar right-triangle geometry.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Confusing a plane's horizontal distance with actual path length
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The slanted path is the hypotenuse, longer than horizontal distance.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Applying trig to an undecomposed nonright polygon
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Basic sine/cosine/tangent right-triangle ratios require a right triangle.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Draw perpendiculars or split the shape into right triangles with justified conditions.

SummaryPoints: Learning goal: decompose polygons into right triangles and solve real-world path/height problems with dimensionally consistent trigonometric equations and units.
Choose correct trigonometric ratios and valid domains; label precise units and approximations.
A complete representation or modelling proof needs teacher review, not a machine-scored scalar.

Lessons.Title: Approximating Pi
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: derive a general inscribed regular n-gon perimeter formula, produce increasing lower approximations to π, and distinguish an approximation from a mathematical bound and proof of convergence.

Official source uses an interactive n-sided polygon exploration and generalizes a formula; the applet is not reproduced. Original geometry/limit explanation is teacher-scored, including limitations of finite n.

Authentic assessment: draw and label the model, independently justify its assumptions and validate precision and units. Teacher rubric (0–4): correct geometric hypotheses, equation or inequality, reasoned calculation, and critical physical/diagram interpretation. Original written and graphical responses are teacher-scored.

Original Edulytiks instruction and examples aligned to Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 4, CC BY 4.0. No publisher logos, artwork or restricted assessment content included.

KeyConcepts.Title: Inscribed chord
KeyConcepts.Definition: A regular n-gon's n vertices on a radius-r circle give central angle 2π/n and each chord length 2r sin(π/n).
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use a central isosceles triangle split into two right triangles.
KeyConcepts.Example: For a unit circle and n=6, each chord length 1.

KeyConcepts.Title: Lower polygon approximation
KeyConcepts.Definition: An inscribed regular n-gon has perimeter P=2nr sin(π/n).
KeyConcepts.Rule: For r=1, π is approximated below by P/2=n sin(π/n).

KeyConcepts.Title: Circumscribed upper bound
KeyConcepts.Definition: A regular circumscribed n-gon tangent to the same circle has half-perimeter nr tan(π/n).
KeyConcepts.Rule: For n≥3, n sin(π/n)<π<n tan(π/n), assuming a Euclidean circle.

WorkedExamples.Title: Inscribed unit hexagon
WorkedExamples.Question: Find the perimeter of a regular hexagon inscribed in radius-1 circle and approximate π.
Steps: Each central triangle has two radius-1 sides with included angle 60° and is equilateral.
Half of unit-circle circumference is π, so P6/2=3 is a lower approximation.
WorkedExamples.Check: This is not an accurate three-decimal estimate.

WorkedExamples.Title: Inscribed decagon
WorkedExamples.Question: Estimate π from a unit-circle regular decagon.
WorkedExamples.Check: Calculator must interpret degrees for sin18°; polygon is inscribed.

WorkedExamples.Title: Prove two-sided bound
WorkedExamples.Question: Show unit circle π lies between inscribed and circumscribed regular hexagon half-perimeters.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use polygon perimeters relative to circle circumference.
Steps: Inscribed hexagon perimeter is 6, so lower half-perimeter 3.
Inscribed polygon is shorter than circle, circumscribed longer: 3<π<2√3.
WorkedExamples.Check: An approximation alone does not prove an exact decimal or a limiting formula.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming a fixed n-gon perimeter equals the circle circumference
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A polygon chord is shorter than the corresponding circular arc.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use a strict lower bound and describe convergence as n increases.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Mixing radius and diameter in circumference comparison
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: C=2πr; half-circumference is πr, not π for arbitrary r.
CommonMistakes.Correction: For unit radius r=1, the half-perimeter estimates π directly.

SummaryPoints: Learning goal: derive a general inscribed regular n-gon perimeter formula, produce increasing lower approximations to π, and distinguish an approximation from a mathematical bound and proof of convergence.
Choose correct trigonometric ratios and valid domains; label precise units and approximations.
A complete representation or modelling proof needs teacher review, not a machine-scored scalar.
